name: Familial Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition Disease
aliases: Familial Calcium Pyrophosphate Dihydrate Crystal Deposition Disease

criteria.description: Identification of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals in synovial fluid by polarized light microscopy
Radiographic evidence of chondrocalcinosis in affected joints
Positive family history of calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease
Episodes of acute or chronic arthritis consistent with CPPD
Identification of pathogenic mutations in genes associated with familial CPPD (e.g., ANKH gene mutations)

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of calcium pyrophosphate crystals in synovial fluid plus radiographic chondrocalcinosis and a positive family history
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Genetic testing can support diagnosis but is not mandatory.

laboratory: Polarized light microscopy showing positively birefringent rhomboid-shaped calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals in synovial fluid
Mildly elevated inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) during acute attacks
imaging: Radiographs showing chondrocalcinosis in articular cartilage, menisci, and fibrocartilage
Occasional MRI showing synovial inflammation and cartilage damage
other: Synovial fluid analysis negative for infection

distinguishingFeatures: Absence of calcium pyrophosphate crystals in synovial fluid
Typically older age of onset without family history
Presence of monosodium urate crystals (needle-shaped, negatively birefringent)
Different joint involvement pattern (e.g., first metatarsophalangeal joint)
Iron overload with elevated serum ferritin and transferrin saturation
Radiographic hook-like osteophytes on metacarpophalangeal joints

redFlags: Rapid joint destruction with severe pain and swelling
Signs of septic arthritis (fever, purulent synovial fluid)
Neurological deficits suggestive of spinal cord or nerve root compression
references: Rosenthal AK, Ryan LM. Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition Disease. N Engl J Med. 2016;374(26):2575-2584.
Zaka-ur-Rab S, et al. Familial chondrocalcinosis: clinical and genetic aspects. Rheumatology (Oxford). 2012;51(3):441-448.
Orphanet: Familial calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (ORPHA:1416)
